questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Functions at Points of Continuity
questions.worked_solution:
The function 

$$
f(x,y,z)=\frac{2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}z}{{x}^{2}+xy+xz-yz}
$$

is continuous except when the denominator is zero. However, the point $(1,1,-2)$ does not cause the denominator to become zero, so we can calculate the limit by substituting  $(1,1,-2)$ into the function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,1,-2)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}z}{{x}^{2}+xy+xz-yz} & =\frac{2\cdot {1}^{2}+{1}^{2}\cdot (-2)}{{1}^{2}+1\cdot 1+1\cdot (-2)-1\cdot (-2)} \\  & =\frac{2-2}{1+1-2+2} \\  & =\frac{0}{2} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Rational Functions by Factoring
questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1,1,2)}\frac{xz+yz}{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} & =\frac{(-1)(2)+1(2)}{(-1)^{2}-{1}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-2+2}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1,1,2)}\frac{xz+yz}{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to (-1,1,2)}\frac{z(x+y)}{(x+y)(x-y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (-1,1,2)}\frac{z\cancel{(x+y)}}{\cancel{(x+y)}(x-y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (-1,1,2)}\frac{z}{x-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1,1,2)}\frac{z}{x-y} & =\frac{2}{-1-1} \\  & =\frac{2}{(-2)} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-1.$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{{x}^{2}+xy+x+y}{xy+{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{x(x+y)+(x+y)}{y(x+y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{(x+1)(x+y)}{y(x+y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{x+1}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{x+1}{y} & =\frac{(-1)+1}{1} \\  & =\frac{0}{1} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $0.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{(x,y,z)\to (1,-1,1)}\frac{2{x}^{2}+xy-{y}^{2}}{z{x}^{2}-z{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{(x,y,z)\to (1,-1,1)}\frac{2{x}^{2}+2xy-xy-{y}^{2}}{z({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})} \\  & ={lim}_{(x,y,z)\to (1,-1,1)}\frac{2x(x+y)-y(x+y)}{z(x+y)(x-y)} \\  & ={lim}_{(x,y,z)\to (1,-1,1)}\frac{(2x-y)(x+y)}{z(x+y)(x-y)} \\  & ={lim}_{(x,y,z)\to (1,-1,1)}\frac{2x-y}{z(x-y)}\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Functions Using Conjugate Multiplication
questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}-3}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}} & =\frac{\sqrt{({0}^{2})({0}^{2})+9}-3}{({0}^{2})({0}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{3-3}{0} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}-3}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{(\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}-3)(\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}+3)}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9-9}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{\cancel{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}}{\cancel{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+9}+3} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{({0}^{2})({0}^{2})+9}+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{9}+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{6}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Functions Using Conjugate Multiplication
questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,0,1)}\frac{x+y-{z}^{2}}{\sqrt{x+y}-z} & =\frac{1+0-{1}^{2}}{\sqrt{1+0}-1} \\  & =\frac{1+0-1}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,0,1)}\frac{x+y-{z}^{2}}{\sqrt{x+y}-z} & ={lim}_{x\to (1,0,1)}\frac{(x+y-{z}^{2})(\sqrt{x+y}+z)}{(\sqrt{x+y}-z)(\sqrt{x+y}+z)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1,0,1)}\frac{(x+y-{z}^{2})(\sqrt{x+y}+z)}{x+y-{z}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1,0,1)}\frac{\cancel{(x+y-{z}^{2})}(\sqrt{x+y}+z)}{\cancel{x+y-{z}^{2}}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1,0,1)}(\sqrt{x+y}+z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,0,1)}(\sqrt{x+y}+z) & =\sqrt{1+0}+1 \\  & =1+0+1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $2.$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,1)}\frac{{x}^{2}-x}{\sqrt{1+xy}-1}=\frac{{0}^{2}-0}{\sqrt{1+0\cdot 1}-1}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,1)}\frac{{x}^{2}-x}{\sqrt{1+xy}-1} & ={lim}_{x\to (0,1)}\frac{({x}^{2}-x)(\sqrt{1+xy}+1)}{(\sqrt{1+xy}-1)(\sqrt{1+xy}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,1)}\frac{x(x-1)(\sqrt{1+xy}+1)}{(\sqrt{1+xy})^{2}-{1}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,1)}\frac{x(x-1)(\sqrt{1+xy}+1)}{xy} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (0,1)}\frac{(x-1)(\sqrt{1+xy}+1)}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,1)}\frac{(x-1)(\sqrt{1+xy}+1)}{y} & =\frac{(0-1)(\sqrt{1+0\cdot 1}+1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{-2}{1} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,1)}-(\sqrt{x}+y) & =-(\sqrt{1}+1) \\  & =-(1+1) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Limits Along Different Paths for Multivariable Functions
questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{2{y}^{2}x+y{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}}=\frac{2\cdot {0}^{2}\cdot 0+0\cdot {0}^{2}}{{0}^{3}+0\cdot {0}^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\frac{2{y}^{2}x+y{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{3}+{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}+{x}^{3}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{3{x}^{3}}{2{x}^{3}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{3}{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=-x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=-x}\frac{2{y}^{2}x+y{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{3}-{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}+{x}^{3}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{3}}{2{x}^{3}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{2{y}^{2}x+y{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}}
$$

- The limit evaluates to $2$ along the path $y=0$
- The limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{3}$ along the path $y=x$
- The limit does not exist
questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}} & =\frac{2({0}^{2})-{0}^{2}}{{0}^{2}+2({0}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{0-0}{0+0} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}-{0}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+2({0}^{2})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2\cancel{{x}^{2}}}{\cancel{{x}^{2}}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is also true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+2{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\cancel{{x}^{2}}}{3\cancel{{x}^{2}}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$

- Statement I is false. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y={x}^{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y={x}^{4}}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}}{{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{4}}}{{x}^{4}+({x}^{4})^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}\cdot {x}^{2}}{{x}^{4}+{x}^{8}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{4}}{{x}^{4}(1+{x}^{4})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2\cancel{{x}^{4}}}{\cancel{{x}^{4}}(1+{x}^{4})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2}{1+{x}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{2}{1+{0}^{4}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $x=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,x=0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}}{{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{2({0}^{2})\sqrt{y}}{{0}^{4}+{y}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}}{{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Limits Along Different Paths for Multivariable Functions
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}
$$

- The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=x$
- The limit evaluates to $1$ along the path $y={x}^{2}$
- The limit exists and is equal to $1$
questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=\frac{{0}^{2}}{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is false. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+(x)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y={x}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y={x}^{2}}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{({x}^{2})}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{x}^{4}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}(1+{x}^{2})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+0} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Functions at Points of Continuity
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The function 

$$
f(x,y)= \dfrac{xy^3}{x+y}
$$

is continuous except when the denominator is zero. However, the point $(-1,2)$ does not cause the denominator to become zero, so we can calculate the limit by substituting  $(-1,2)$ into the function:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1,2)}\frac{x{y}^{3}}{x+y} & =\frac{(-1)\cdot {2}^{3}}{(-1)+2} \\  & =\frac{-8}{1} \\  & =-8\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Rational Functions by Factoring
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac 0 0,$ as follows:

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (-1,1)}} \dfrac{x^2y+xy^2}{x^2-y^2} = \dfrac{(-1)^2(1) + (-1)(1)^2}{(-1)^2 - (1)^2} = \dfrac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{xy(x+y)}{(x+y)(x-y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{xy}{(x-y)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{xy}{(x-y)} & =\frac{(-1)\cdot 1}{-1-1} \\  & =\frac{-1}{-2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $\dfrac{1}{2}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Functions Using Conjugate Multiplication
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac00,$ as follows: 

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,1)}} \dfrac{2^2-4 \cdot 1}{2-2\sqrt{1}} = \dfrac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{{x}^{2}-4y}{x-2\sqrt{y}} & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{({x}^{2}-4y)(x+2\sqrt{y})}{(x-2\sqrt{y})(x+2\sqrt{y})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{({x}^{2}-4y)(x+2\sqrt{y})}{{x}^{2}-(2\sqrt{y})^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{({x}^{2}-4y)(x+2\sqrt{y})}{{x}^{2}-4y} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1)}(x+2\sqrt{y})\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,1)}(x+2\sqrt{y}) & =2+2\sqrt{1} \\  & =2+2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $4.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Limits Along Different Paths for Multivariable Functions
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Direct substitution gives an indeterminate form, but the function cannot be simplified by canceling a common factor in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}} \dfrac{x(x + 2y)}{y^2} = \dfrac{0 \cdot (0 + 2 \cdot 0)}{0^2} = \dfrac{0}{0}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Taking $\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\frac{x(x+2y)}{{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(x+2x)}{{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{3{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)$ along the path $y=-x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=-x}\frac{x(x+2y)}{{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(x+2(-x))}{(-x)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{-{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on these two paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
\displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}} \dfrac{x(x + 2y)}{y^2} = \text{DNE}
$$
